images.text:
Vanessa: Now that I've got some food in my stomach, I might be able to tackle this head-on again.
Sally: Great! I must keep an open mind and be sure to consider all the possibilities.
Vanessa: So, you have to explain to me why you think floristry is a good choice for you to study.
Sally: Okay. First of all, I really love flowers and plants. And, I'm good at taking care of them. I've got a green thumb! My mother also loved flowers and I grew up surrounded by them. Don't you think that's a good reason?

Vanessa: Yes, that's a good reason, but it can't be the only one. You have to come up with several more motives.
Sally: Sure. Working with plants and having them around me makes me feel happy and serene.
Vanessa: Yes, it must be wonderful to be surrounded by green life all day. And I know you really love the smell of flowers.
Sally: I do! Wouldn't it be great to be paid to be with plants and flowers all day?
Vanessa: Yeah, it really would be great.

Sally: So ... admit it. Isn't it a great idea?
Vanessa: Well, I admit ... it does sound like it could be a perfect job for you. But aren't you worried that changing your career now is not the right move?
Sally: YOLO, Vanessa, YOLO.
Vanessa: What does that mean?
Sally: You only live once!

Modals for Possibility and Necessity
You use modals when you want to express possibility and necessity.
You use may, might and could to express possibility in the past and in the future.
*Might suggests that something is less possible than may or could.

• might / might not + infinitive
  • could / could not + infinitive
  • may / may not + infinitive
Expressing Necessity
You use must or have to to express that something is necessarily true.

Example:
I must keep an open mind and be sure to consider all the possibilities.
I might be able to tackle this head-on again.
I must keep an open mind and be sure to consider all the possibilities.
You have to explain to me why you think floristry is a good choice for you to study.
You have to come up with several more motives.
It could be a perfect job for you.
Negative Questions To Encourage Agreement
Negative questions have a different meaning than regular questions.
A negative question can have two different meanings. It can, for example, be used to ask for confirmation of something you believe to be true.
• Didn't you see Ann yesterday? How is she doing? ( = I believe that you saw Ann yesterday.)
You may also express your opinions and encourage agreement in a more polite way.
• Wouldn't it be nice to paint that wall green? (More polite than ‘It would be nice to paint that wall green.')
Don't you think that's a good reason?
Wouldn't it be great to be paid to be with plants and flowers all day?
Isn't it a great idea?
But aren't you worried that changing your career now is not the right move?
Contracted and uncontracted negative questions have a different word order. Uncontracted negative questions are usually used in a formal style.</br></br>Examples:</br>
Aren't you leaving? (Contracted – auxiliary verb + n't + subject)
Doesn't he know? (Auxiliary verb + n't + subject)
Are you not interested? (Uncontracted – auxiliary verb + subject + not)
Does he not understand the plan? (Auxiliary verb + subject + not)

These are words you use to talk about feelings, reactions and decision-making.
to keep an open mind
to be willing to take into account different opinions or ideas
(expression)
Example: I must keep an open mind and be sure to consider all the possibilities.
engenn8le18ob06aud02
to have a green thumb
to be good at growing plants
(expression)
Example: I really love flowers and plants. And, I'm good at taking care of them. I've got a green thumb!
engenn8le18ob06aud03
to come up with
to be able to find or improvise something
(phrasal verb)
Example: You have to come up with several more motives if you want to decide to study floristry.
engenn8le18ob06aud04
motive
an incentive someone has for doing something
(noun)
Example: You have to find several more motives for making a decision.
engenn8le18ob06aud05
serene
to be calm and peaceful
(adjective)
Example: Working with plants and having them around me makes me feel happy and serene.
engenn8le18ob06aud06
the right move
the best direction or option someone has or can find
(expression)
Example: But aren't you worried that changing your career now is not the right move?

Write a letter to a friend describing a big decision you want to make. You can invent a situation.
In your letter, be sure to have at least three reasons (pros) for why you think this is a good thing for you to do.
Exchange your letter with a partner.
After you read your partner's letter, write a letter back to your partner. In your letter you will “play the devil's advocate”.
For each reason your partner gives to make the change, give reasons (cons) that they should not make this change.
Give your response letter to your partner.
